subject: surgery
title: Commando Operation, Neck Dissection Classifications, and Ranula

steps.tx: Locally advanced carcinoma of the oral cavity involving the tongue, floor of mouth, and adjacent mandible demands aggressive composite surgical extirpation. The classic composite resection is famously known as the **commando operation**, an acronym representing Combined Mandibulectomy and Neck Dissection with oral lesion excision in-continuity. Originally named after the daring commando raids of the Second World War, the procedure achieves en bloc oncological clearance of the primary tumor and primary draining lymphatic basin.
steps.say: The commando operation is a composite resection combining mandibulectomy, oral tumor excision, and neck dissection in one continuous specimen. It provides definitive oncological clearance for locally advanced oral cancer.

nodes.label: Advanced Oral Tumor with Mandibular Invasion
Cervical Neck Dissection (Levels I to V)

steps.tx: This operative plan removes cheek tumour, a segment of mandible and the neck nodes as one continuous specimen rather than separate pieces. That is the essence of the **commando operation**, designed so tumour is never cut across while clearing its draining basin. The resulting defect explains why fibular reconstruction and dental rehabilitation are planned before the first incision.
steps.say: The commando operation removes tumour, mandible and neck nodes in one continuous specimen. Reconstruction is planned before incision.

steps.tx: Following a commando resection, loss of mandibular bone continuity produces severe cosmetic deformity and the functional handicap known as Andy Gump deformity, where the unsupported chin falls backward. To restore dental occlusion, facial projection, and mastication, modern reconstructive surgery utilizes a **free fibula flap**. The vascularized fibular osteocutaneous flap, based on the peroneal artery and venae comitantes, permits multiple osteotomies to accurately contour the neo-mandible while providing skin for intraoral lining.
steps.say: Segmental mandibulectomy causes severe chin collapse. Reconstruction with a vascularized free fibula flap based on the peroneal vessels restores the mandibular arch and supports dental implants.

steps.tx: Surgical management of cervical lymph node metastases follows standardized anatomical classifications. The historical benchmark was the **radical neck dissection**, codified by George Crile. This extensive procedure removes all lymphatic tissue from levels one through five along with three non-lymphatic structures: the internal jugular vein, the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and the spinal accessory nerve. Sacrificing the accessory nerve leads to severe shoulder drop and chronic trapezius neuropathic pain.
steps.say: Radical neck dissection excises cervical nodal levels one through five along with three non-lymphatic structures: the accessory nerve, internal jugular vein, and sternocleidomastoid muscle.

points: Clears all lymph node levels from level I to level V
Routinely sacrifices spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)

right.title: Modified Radical Neck Dissection
points: Clears all lymph node levels from level I to level V

steps.tx: To reduce functional and cosmetic morbidity without compromising oncological cure, surgeons developed the **modified radical neck dissection**. By definition, this operation removes all lymph node groups from levels one through five while preserving one or more of the non-lymphatic structures routinely resected in radical neck dissection. Preservation of the spinal accessory nerve maintains trapezius motor function, preventing shoulder abduction weakness, while sparing the internal jugular vein avoids venous hypertension.
steps.say: Modified radical neck dissection clears nodal levels one through five while preserving one or more non-lymphatic structures. Preserving the accessory nerve prevents debilitating shoulder drop.

rows: Internal jugular vein and sternocleidomastoid muscle resected
Spinal accessory nerve and internal jugular vein preserved
Spinal accessory nerve, internal jugular vein, and SCM all preserved
Only lymphatic tissue of levels I through V excised fascial-plane

steps.tx: In patients with clinically node-negative necks presenting with early-stage oral cancer, an elective **selective neck dissection** is preferred over comprehensive nodal clearance. For oral cavity primaries, the standard procedure is a supraomohyoid neck dissection, which removes only levels one, two, and three, preserving levels four and five. If frozen section examination demonstrates unexpected metastatic involvement in these nodes, the dissection is immediately converted to a comprehensive modified radical clearance.
steps.say: Selective neck dissection removes only the primary draining nodal basins. For oral cavity tumors, supraomohyoid neck dissection clears levels one, two, and three, sparing other groups.

steps.tx: Benign cystic swellings in the sublingual space frequently present diagnostic dilemmas. A **ranula** is a translucent, bluish extravasation pseudocyst arising in the floor of the mouth, historically likened to the translucent underbelly of a frog. It develops when traumatic ductal rupture or chronic inflammation in the sublingual salivary gland allows continuous leakage of viscous saliva into surrounding submucosal tissues. Because it lacks an epithelial lining, it is a pseudocyst.
steps.say: A ranula is a bluish, translucent extravasation pseudocyst arising from the sublingual salivary gland in the floor of the mouth. Trauma allows mucus to pool in the submucosa, resembling a frog belly.

steps.tx: Lift the tongue and this dome shines translucent blue, like a small frog belly beneath the mucosa. A **ranula** is leaked sublingual saliva collecting as a pseudocyst, so its wall has no true epithelial lining. Simple drainage always refills; lasting cure means dealing with the feeding sublingual gland, either by marsupialisation in selected cases or gland excision.
steps.say: A translucent bluish floor-of-mouth dome indicates a ranula from leaked sublingual saliva. Drainage alone always refills.

vis.alt: Intraoral ranula showing a translucent bluish cystic swelling in the floor of the mouth
vis.caption: Intraoral ranula showing a translucent bluish cystic swelling in the floor of the mouth. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: When saliva from a leaking sublingual gland tracks around the free posterior border of the mylohyoid muscle or penetrates through congenital mylohyoid boutons, it enters the neck, forming a **plunging ranula**. Patients present with a soft, doughy, painless mass in the submandibular triangle that fluctuates on bimanual palpation. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging demonstrates the classic tail sign, showing the cystic neck lesion tapering into the sublingual space.
steps.say: A plunging ranula herniates past the mylohyoid muscle into the submandibular neck space. Cross-sectional imaging reveals the pathognomonic tail sign tapering back toward the sublingual gland.

nodes.label: Tracts Behind Free Posterior Edge of Mylohyoid

steps.tx: Management of a ranula has evolved away from simple incision, aspiration, or marsupialization, which suffer prohibitive recurrence rates exceeding sixty to eighty percent. Definitive cure mandates **sublingual gland excision**, removing the offending salivary source. For a simple oral ranula, transoral excision of the ipsilateral sublingual gland is sufficient. For an extensive plunging ranula, a combined transoral and transcervical approach allows complete evacuation of the cervical pseudocyst alongside sublingual gland removal.
steps.say: Simple drainage or marsupialization leads to frequent recurrence. Permanent cure demands complete surgical excision of the underlying sublingual salivary gland through a transoral or transcervical approach.
